claim: Natural populations of Arabidopsis thaliana persist in complex environments where biotic stressors such as pathogen and insect communities fluctuate temporally and spatially.
source: Natural populations persist in complex environments, where biotic stressors, such as pathogen and insect communities, fluctuate temporally and spatially.
evidence: This is a general statement about natural populations and their environments, drawing on established ecological knowledge.

claim: Shifting biotic pressures generate heterogeneous selective forces that can maintain standing natural variation within a species.
source: These shifting biotic pressures generate heterogeneous selective forces that can maintain standing natural variation within a species.
evidence: This statement is based on evolutionary theory about how environmental heterogeneity affects genetic variation.

claim: Variation in naturally polymorphic GSL genes affected fitness in each environment tested.
source: we found that variation in these naturally polymorphic GSL genes affected fitness in each of our environments
evidence: This claim is supported by the field trial data presented in the manuscript showing fitness effects across environments.

claim: The fitness pattern of GSL genotypes fluctuated such that highly fit genotypes in one trial displayed lower fitness in another.
source: the pattern fluctuated such that highly fit genotypes in one trial displayed lower fitness in another
evidence: This is supported by the fitness measurements across different field trials shown in the results.

claim: No GSL genotype or genotypes consistently out-performed the others across all environments.
source: no GSL genotype or genotypes consistently out-performed the others
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the fitness data across multiple environments presented in the study.

claim: The fitness pattern fluctuation was true both across locations and within the same location across years.
source: This was true both across locations and within the same location across years.
evidence: This is supported by comparing results from UWY 2011 and UWY 2012 (same location, different years) and between UWY and UCD (different locations).

claim: Environmental heterogeneity may contribute to the maintenance of GSL variation observed within Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: These results indicate that environmental heterogeneity may contribute to the maintenance of GSL variation observed within Arabidopsis thaliana.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed fitness fluctuations across environments.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana exhibits high levels of standing variation among natural populations and accessions.
source: This is particularly true for the model species Arabidopsis thaliana, which exhibits variation both within and among natural populations and/or accessions (Pigliucci and Marlow, 2001; Atwell et al., 2010; Bomblies et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2010; Platt et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2011; Debieu et al., 2013; Joseph et al., 2013; Long et al., 2013; Anwer et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Mutation-selection balance theory predicts that observed variation will be due to rare alleles at many loci introduced through random mutations that evolution acts on to eliminate through persistent purifying natural selection.
source: Models based on mutation-selection balance theory predict that this observed variation will be due to rare alleles at many loci introduced through random mutations that evolution acts on to eliminate through persistent purifying natural selection (Kimura, 1968; Turelli, 1984).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from cited evolutionary models.

claim: Studies of nucleotide variation in Arabidopsis have found an excess of low frequency polymorphisms relative to expectation.
source: In agreement, studies of nucleotide variation in Arabidopsis have found an excess of low frequency polymorphisms relative to expectation (Purugganan & Suddith, 1998, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Studies cloning causal genetic variants from natural Arabidopsis accessions have found several examples of intermediate frequency alleles maintained at polymorphic loci.
source: However, other studies cloning causal genetic variants from natural Arabidopsis accessions have found several intriguing examples of intermediate frequency alleles maintained at polymorphic loci (Johanson et al., 2000; Long et al., 2000; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The neutral theory posits that the majority of genetic polymorphisms have no effect on fitness.
source: The neutral theory posits that the majority of genetic polymorphisms have no effect on fitness and that stochastic evolutionary processes, such as genetic drift and migration, are sufficient to explain the genetic and phenotypic variation observed within and among populations (Darwin, 1859; Kimura, 1968; Duret, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of neutral theory supported by citations.

claim: For many ecologically important traits, phenotypic variation has been shown to empirically impact fitness in natural populations.
source: However, for many ecologically important traits, phenotypic variation has been shown to empirically impact fitness in natural populations, suggesting that natural selection also plays an important role in the evolution of such traits (Mothershead and Marquis, 2000; Adler et al., 2001; Tian et al., 2003; Korves et al., 2007; Milla et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Arabidopsis has become a key model system suitable for characterizing, cloning and validating genes influencing the fitness consequences of underlying natural variation.
source: A. thaliana has become a key model system and is extremely suitable for characterizing, cloning and validating genes influencing the fitness consequences of underlying natural variation.
evidence: This is based on the known characteristics and resources available for Arabidopsis research.

claim: Arabidopsis persists in many different environments and experiences selection from both abiotic pressures and biotic pressures that vary temporally and spatially.
source: Arabidopsis persists in many different environments and experiences selection from both abiotic pressures, such as temperature and precipitation, and biotic pressures, such as insect and pathogen populations that vary temporally and spatially (Meyerowitz, 1987; Richards et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Arabidopsis has evolved high levels of natural variation among accessions for many important phenotypic traits, including glucosinolates.
source: Potentially to maximize fitness across a broad range of biotia, Arabidopsis has evolved high levels of natural variation among accessions for many important phenotypic traits, including the defense compounds, glucosinolates (GSLs) (Stahl et al., 1999; Atwell et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Glucosinolates constitute a diverse set of plant-made defensive metabolites restricted primarily to the Brassicales.
source: GSLs constitute a diverse set of plant-made defensive metabolites restricted primarily to the Brassicales
evidence: This is established knowledge about glucosinolates.

claim: Glucosinolates are partitioned into three classes (indolic, aliphatic and aromatic) depending on their amino acid precursor.
source: that are partitioned into three classes, indolic, aliphatic and aromatic, depending on their amino acid precursor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about glucosinolate classification.

claim: Natural genetic polymorphisms found among a suite of aliphatic GSL genes in Arabidopsis are responsible for the majority of GSL diversity observed in the leaf tissue.
source: Natural genetic polymorphisms found among a suite of aliphatic GSL genes in Arabidopsis are responsible for the majority of GSL diversity observed in the leaf tissue (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the biosynthetic pathway diagram in Figure 1 and references to previous studies.

claim: Aliphatic GSL genes encode enzymes, transcription factors and activation co-factors that have been identified, cloned and validated in a laboratory setting.
source: These aliphatic GSL genes encode enzymes, transcription factors and activation co-factors that have been identified, cloned and validated in a laboratory setting (Table 1) (Haughn et al., 1991; Li and Quiros, 2003; Hansen et al., 2007, 2008; Hirai et al., 2007; Li et al., 2008; Neal et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by Table 1 and citations to published studies.

claim: Previous studies have uncovered links between GSL variation and ecologically important traits in Arabidopsis such as resistance to insect/pathogen damage, flowering time, and growth.
source: Previous studies have uncovered links between GSL variation and ecologically important traits in Arabidopsis, such as resistance to insect/pathogen damage, flowering time, and growth, suggesting that GSLs play an important role in determining plant fitness (Mauricio, 1998; Kliebenstein et al., 2002; Bidart-Bouzat and Kliebenstein, 2008; Hansen et al., 2008; Burow et al., 2010; Kerwin et al., 2011; Züst et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The transcription factors MYB28 and MYB29 control accumulation of aliphatic GLS.
source: The transcription factors MYB28 and MYB29 control accumulation of aliphatic GLS.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by citations in Table 1.

claim: A double knockout in MYB28 and MYB29 results in no aliphatic GLS accumulation.
source: A double knockout in these genes results in no aliphatic GLS accumulation
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by experimental data.

claim: A single knockout in MYB29 leads to a 25% reduction in aliphatic GSL compared to WT Col-0.
source: or a 25% reduction in aliphatic GSL (myb29), compared to WT Col-0.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by experimental data.

claim: Variation at the Elong locus controls the number of carbons added to the amino acid precursor and therefore the length of the GSL side chain.
source: Variation at the Elong locus controls the number of carbons added to the amino acid precursor and therefore, the length of the GSL side chain, R.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by citations.

claim: A functional allele at the MAM1 locus leads primarily to accumulation of GSL with four carbon (4C) length side chains.
source: A functional allele at this locus, MAM1, leads primarily to accumulation of GSL with four carbon (4C) length side chains
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by experimental data.

claim: A non-functional MAM1 allele (gsm1) leads to accumulation of GSL with three carbon (3C) length side chains.
source: whereas a non-functional allele, gsm1 leads to accumulation of GSL with three carbon (3C) length side chains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by experimental data.

claim: GSOX1 and GSOX3 oxygenate a methylthio (MT) to methylsulfinyl (MSO) GSL.
source: GSOX1 & GSOX3 oxygenate a methylthio (MT) to methylsulfinyl (MSO) GSL.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supported by citations.

claim: AOP2 converts MSO to alkenyl GSL such as allyl and but-3-enyl.
source: AOP2 converts MSO to alkenyl, such as allyl and but-3-enyl.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supported by citations.

claim: AOP3 converts only 3C length MSO to OH-propyl GSL and cannot act on the 4MSO GSL.
source: AOP3, on the other hand converts only 3C length MSO to OH-propyl GSL and cannot act on the 4MSO GSL.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supported by citations.

claim: GSOH oxygenates the 4C but-3-enyl to the OH-alkenyl GSL, OH-but-3-enyl.
source: GSOH oxygenates the 4C but-3-enyl to the OH-alkenyl GSL, OH-but-3-enyl.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supported by citations.

claim: A functional AOP2 is necessary for GSOH to function, making AOP2 epistatic to GSOH.
source: Since GSOH acts on but-3-enyl GSL, which is a product of AOP2, a functional AOP2 is necessary for GSOH to function and AOP2 is said to be epistatic to GSOH.
evidence: This is an inference from the biosynthetic pathway shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Col-0 is functional for MAM1 and the GSOX's, null for both AOP2 and AOP3, and functional for GSOH, resulting in accumulation of primarily 4MSO GLS.
source: Col-0 is functional for MAM1 and the GSOX's, null for both AOP2 and AOP3, and functional for GSOH, resulting in accumulation of primarily 4MSO GLS.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supported by experimental data.

claim: Upon cellular disruption, GLS come into contact with their own plant-made activating enzyme, myrosinase.
source: Upon cellular disruption, such as occurs during pathogen attack, insect herbivory or even wind damage, GLS come into contact with their own plant-made activating enzyme, myrosinase.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and is established knowledge about GSL activation.

claim: Myrosinase activates the GSL compound by cleaving the glucose moiety, yielding an unstable aglycone structure.
source: Myrosinase activates the GSL compound by cleaving the glucose moiety, yielding an unstable aglycone structure that non-enzymatically rearranges to either nitriles or isothiocyanates, depending on the presence of the co-activators ESM1 and ESP.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and is established knowledge about GSL activation.

claim: The synthetic laboratory population varies at specific genes controlling aliphatic GSL variation within a single common genetic background.
source: This synthetic laboratory population varies at specific genes controlling aliphatic GSL variation within a single common genetic background.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the synthetic population created for the study.

claim: Field trials were conducted at the University of California, Davis in Spring 2012 and the University of Wyoming in Summer 2011 and Summer 2012.
source: We transplanted 2 week old, greenhouse-germinated replicates of the synthetic laboratory population into the field at the University of California, Davis in Davis, CA in Spring 2012 and the University of Wyoming in Laramie, WY in Summer 2011 and Summer 2012.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and locations.

claim: Genotypes were replicated in 40 randomized blocks in the field in each of the three field trials.
source: In each of our three field trials, which represent three environments, genotypes were replicated in 40 randomized blocks in the field, for a total of 120 blocks/replicates.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Half of the blocks in each field trial were treated with pesticides and the other half were not.
source: To distinguish the effects of GSL variation alone from the interaction of GSL variation with field herbivory as well as assess the effects of leaf damage in the field, half of the blocks in each field trial were treated with pesticides and the other half were not (Figure 3) (Mauricio, 1998).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 3.

claim: The majority of variation in GSL profiles in the field was controlled by the GSL genotypes.
source: A mixed model analysis of field GSL revealed that the majority of variation in GSL profiles in the field was controlled by the GSL genotypes that we generated (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: The majority of the GSL genotypes produced the expected GSL profiles in the field, consistent with lab studies.
source: Importantly, the majority of the GSL genotypes produced the expected GSL profiles in the field, consistent with the lab studies (Figure 4 and Figure 1—figure supplements 1–17).
evidence: This is supported by the GSL profile data shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: The scores for the field grown genotypes were highly correlated with the lab grown genotypes, showing that the GSL genetic variation leads to highly similar field and lab profiles.
source: The scores for the field grown genotypes were highly correlated with the lab grown genotypes, showing that the GSL genetic variation leads to highly similar field and lab profiles (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: All lines harboring a functional AOP2 gene produce alkenyl GSL (e.g., but-3-enyl GSL).
source: For example, all lines harboring a functional AOP2 gene produce alkenyl GSL (e.g., but-3-enyl GSL) (Figures 1, 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: The functional/non-functional allelic state at the MAM1 locus was always predictive of the chain-length of the GSL in the field.
source: Additionally, the functional/non-functional allelic state at the MAM1 locus was always predictive of the chain-length of the GSL in the field as predicted from lab experiments.
evidence: This is supported by the GSL profile data from field experiments.

claim: Lines with a functional MAM1 produced more 4C GSL than 3C GSL, while genotypes with a non-functional MAM1 always produced more 3C GSL than 4C GSL.
source: The lines with a functional MAM1, like Col-0, produced more 4C GSL than 3C GSL, while genotypes with a non-functional MAM1 always produced more 3C GSL than 4C GSL (Figure 4) (Haughn et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4 and cited literature.

claim: A functional copy of GSOH always leads to the production of 2-OH-but-3-enyl GSL from but-3-enyl GSL.
source: A functional copy of GSOH, the gene encoding the enzyme to create 2-OH-but-3-enyl, always leads to the production of 2-OH-but-3-enyl GSL from but-3-enyl GSL (Figures 1, 4) (Hansen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 1 and 4 and cited literature.

claim: A non-functional MYB28 leads to an almost complete reduction in long chain (8C) GSL and a 60% reduction in short chain (3C and 4C) GSL.
source: Specifically, a non-functional MYB28 leads to an almost complete reduction in long chain (8C) GSL and a 60% reduction in short chain (3C and 4C) GSL (Figure 4) (Hirai et al., 2007; Sønderby et al., 2007, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4 and cited literature.

claim: A non-functional MYB29 leads to a 40% reduction in short chain GSL with no significant reduction in long chain GSL.
source: A non-functional MYB29 leads to a 40% reduction in short chain GSL with no significant reduction in long chain GSL (Figure 4) (Hirai et al., 2007; Sønderby et al., 2007, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4 and cited literature.

claim: A double mutant in MYB28 and MYB29 lead to an almost complete loss of all aliphatic GSLs.
source: A double mutant in MYB28 and MYB29 lead to an almost complete loss of all aliphatic GSLs, as expected (Figure 4) (Hirai et al., 2007; Sønderby et al., 2007, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4 and cited literature.

claim: In the field there was no measureable accumulation of MT GSL in any line, likely due to the redundant function of the GSOX2 and GSOX4 genes.
source: In the field there was no measureable accumulation of MT GSL in any line, likely due to the redundant function of the GSOX2 and GSOX4 genes (Kerwin et al., 2011, 2012; Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the field data and cited literature about gene redundancy.

claim: The field results show that the laboratory work on GSL genotypes and their associated GSL profiles are translatable and predictive of the GSL profiles found in naturally fluctuating environments.
source: Thus, the field results show that the laboratory work on GSL genotypes and their associated GSL profiles are translatable and predictive of the GSL profiles found in naturally fluctuating environments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing field and lab GSL profile data.

claim: The specific composition of GLSs within a genotype largely did not change across the environments.
source: The specific composition of GLSs within a genotype largely did not change across the environments (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: The total amount of aliphatic GSL content showed a significant genotype by environment effect.
source: In contrast, the total amount of aliphatic GSL content, that is, the sum of all aliphatic GSLs per sample, showed a significant genotype by environment effect, indicating that impact of environment on total aliphatic GSL accumulation varied among the different GSL genotypes in this study (Table 3 and Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 3 and the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The AOP2 genotype showed a dramatic variation in total aliphatic GSL across the three field trials.
source: For example, the AOP2 genotype showed a dramatic variation in total aliphatic GSL across the three field trials (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Genotypes with a myb28/myb29 double knockout accumulated virtually no GSL in all three environments.
source: For example, genotypes with a myb28/myb29 double knockout accumulated virtually no GSL in all three environments.
evidence: This is supported by the GSL accumulation data across environments.

claim: The GSL genotype is the dominant determinant of GSL profile in the field.
source: Thus, the GSL genotype is the dominant determinant of GSL profile in the field
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GSL profile data across environments.

claim: Total aliphatic GSL accumulation is determined by an interaction of genotype and environment within the laboratory population.
source: while total aliphatic GSL accumulation is determined by an interaction of genotype and environment within our laboratory population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of GSL accumulation data.

claim: Leaf damage significantly varied across the three environments.
source: A mixed model analysis showed that leaf damage significantly varied across the three environments but that the pesticide application did not significantly alter leaf damage in the field (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: The pesticide application did not significantly alter leaf damage in the field.
source: A mixed model analysis showed that leaf damage significantly varied across the three environments but that the pesticide application did not significantly alter leaf damage in the field (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: The UWY2012 field trial had significantly higher levels of leaf damage than both UWY2011 and UCD2012.
source: The UWY2012 field trial (mean = 2.610) had significantly higher levels of leaf damage than both UWY2011 (mean = 1.17, p value <1e-04) and UCD2012 (mean = 1.50, p value <1e-04)
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparison of leaf damage across environments.

claim: UCD2012 and UWY2011 environments did not differ significantly for leaf damage.
source: though UCD2012 and UWY2011 environments did not differ significantly for leaf damage (p value = 0.44).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparison of leaf damage.

claim: There is no significant correlation of leaf damage across the three environments.
source: In fact, we see no significant correlation of leaf damage across the three environments (Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Table 5.

claim: The three environments experienced differing herbivory pressures.
source: This suggests the three environments experienced differing herbivory pressures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation in leaf damage across environments.

claim: The UWY field site showed both the highest and lowest leaf damage levels, demonstrating that there can be potentially large temporal fluctuations in herbivory at a single location.
source: It is interesting to note that the UWY field site showed both the highest and lowest leaf damage levels, demonstrating that there can be potentially large temporal fluctuations in herbivory at a single location (Table 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the leaf damage data across years at the same location.

claim: Within a field environment, levels of leaf damage significantly varied across GSL genotypes.
source: Within a field environment, levels of leaf damage significantly varied across GSL genotypes, in agreement with the role of GSL in deterring herbivory (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: The extent of leaf damage incurred upon different GSL genotypes in the field fluctuated among environments, such that no particular GSL genotype showed a consistent maximal or minimal level of leaf damage across the three field trials.
source: However, the extent of leaf damage incurred upon different GSL genotypes in the field fluctuated among environments, such that no particular GSL genotype showed a consistent maximal or minimal level of leaf damage across the three field trials (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the leaf damage data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The myb28/AOP2 and AOP2 genotypes had similar herbivory in UCD2012 and UWY2011 but strongly diverged in UWY2012.
source: For example, the myb28/AOP2 and AOP2 genotypes had similar herbivory in UCD2012 (mean = 1.30 and 1.95, respectively) and UWY2011 (mean = 1.29 and 0.80, respectively) but strongly diverged in UWY2012 (mean = 1.45 and 5.64, respectively) (Figure 6 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the leaf damage data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The extent to which GSL profile provides resistance varies across different herbivore species in a laboratory setting.
source: It has been shown, in a laboratory setting that the extent to which GSL profile provides resistance varies across different herbivore species (Kroymann et al., 2003; Pfalz et al., 2007; Hansen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: GSL have been shown to provide resistance to fungi, bacteria and nematodes.
source: In addition, GSL have been shown to provide resistance to fungi, bacteria and nematodes, which may have also been present and variable between our environments (Manici et al., 1997; Tierens et al., 2001; Aires et al., 2009; Witzel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: GSL variation controls differential leaf damage in each field trial but the specific directions of effect for individual GSL genotypes is subject to environmental conditions.
source: Together, these results show that GSL variation controls differential leaf damage in each field trial but the specific directions of effect for individual GSL genotypes is subject to environmental conditions, such as the composition of herbivores, which can vary temporally and spatially.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the leaf damage data across environments.

claim: Total fruit count (TFC) has previously been shown to be a good proxy for fecundity in Arabidopsis where total number of seeds per plant is highly correlated with total number of siliques.
source: TFC has previously been shown to be a good proxy for fecundity in Arabidopsis where total number of seeds per plant is highly correlated with total number of siliques (i.e., fruits) (Wolf et al., 2000; Kliebenstein et al., 2001c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: There was significant variation in silique length across GSL genotypes as well as a significant genotype by environment interaction.
source: However, there was significant variation in silique length across GSL genotypes as well as a significant genotype by environment interaction (Table 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis in the supplementary data.

claim: GSL genotype had a significant impact on absolute field fitness.
source: In this study, GSL genotype had a significant impact on absolute field fitness (Table 6).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 6.

claim: There was a significant interaction effect between GSL genotype and environment for absolute fitness both including and excluding survivorship.
source: There was also a significant interaction effect between GSL genotype and environment for absolute fitness both including and excluding survivorship, suggesting that the impact that GSL genotype has on fitness is conditioned upon the environment (Table 6).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 6.

claim: Environment did not show a significant main effect on either measure of absolute fitness.
source: Environment did not show a significant main effect on either measure of absolute fitness, suggesting that the population mean for absolute fitness may have been comparable across the environments
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 6.

claim: GSL genotypes that recreate natural variation within a single common genetic background influence field fitness of A. thaliana in an environmentally dependent manner.
source: Thus, these GSL genotypes that recreate natural variation within a single common genetic background influence field fitness of A. thaliana in an environmentally dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fitness data across environments.

claim: Absolute fitness varied greatly between the highest and lowest ranked GSL genotypes within each of the environments.
source: Absolute fitness varied greatly between the highest and lowest ranked GSL genotypes within each of the environments (Figure 7 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the fitness data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The performance of different GSL genotypes relative to each other varied across environments, so that no GSL genotype outperformed all the others in all three environments.
source: In addition, the performance of different GSL genotypes relative to each other varied across environments, so that no GSL genotype outperformed all the others in all three environments.
evidence: This is supported by the fitness data across environments.

claim: myb28/AOP2 shows the greatest fitness in the UCD2012 environment and the lowest fitness in UWY2012.
source: For example, myb28/AOP2 shows the greatest fitness in the UCD2012 environment and the lowest fitness in UWY2012.
evidence: This is supported by the fitness data shown in Figure 7.

claim: myb28/gsoh shows an opposite pattern to myb28/AOP2 in fitness across environments.
source: In contrast, myb28/gsoh shows an opposite pattern
evidence: This is supported by the fitness data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The significant interaction of GSL genotype by environment controlling fitness is caused by fluctuations in the fitness rank of different genotypes across environments.
source: Thus, it appears that the significant interaction of GSL genotype by environment controlling fitness is caused by fluctuations in the fitness rank of different genotypes across environments (Figure 7 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fitness data shown in Figure 7.

claim: GSL genotype and the interaction between GSL genotype and environment both had a significant impact on relative fitness in the field both including and excluding survivorship.
source: Even more strongly than with our absolute fitness measurements, we found that GSL genotype and the interaction between GSL genotype and environment both had a significant impact on relative fitness in the field both including and excluding survivorship (Table 6).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 6.

claim: myb28 has a higher than average relative fitness in UWY2011 but shows an average and slightly lower than average relative fitness in UWY2012 and UCD2012, respectively.
source: For example, myb28 has a higher than average relative fitness in UWY2011 but shows an average and slightly lower than average relative fitness in UWY2012 and UCD2012, respectively (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the relative fitness data shown in Figure 8.

claim: myb28/AOP2 has low relative fitness in both UWY field trials but higher relative fitness in UCD.
source: Two examples, with opposite patterns are myb28/AOP2, that has low relative fitness in both UWY field trials but higher relative fitness in UCD
evidence: This is supported by the relative fitness data.

claim: gsm1 has high relative fitness in both UWY field trials but lower relative fitness in UCD.
source: and gsm1, that has high relative fitness in both UWY field trials but lower relative fitness in UCD.
evidence: This is supported by the relative fitness data.

claim: Temporal and spatial fluctuations in fitness can both occur and are dependent on genotypic differences.
source: This indicates that temporal and spatial fluctuations in fitness can both occur and are dependent on genotypic differences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fitness data across environments and years.

claim: In both absolute and relative fitness measures, UCD2012 clusters with UWY2011 and the two UWY field trials do not cluster together.
source: In both cases, UCD2012 clusters with UWY2011 and the two UWY field trials do not cluster together, showing that within an environment across years there is the potential for greater variability than across environments.
evidence: This is supported by the hierarchical clustering shown in Figure 8.

claim: Both flowering time and total indole GSL in the field were significantly affected by the GSL genetic variation in the synthetic population.
source: In the field, both of these phenotypes were significantly affected by the GSL genetic variation in our synthetic population, indicating that aliphatic GSL genes can have pleiotropic impacts beyond the aliphatic GSL pathway that can be observed in natural settings (Table 3 and Table 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: There was no significant correlation between absolute fitness and pleiotropic traits (flowering time and total indole GSL) in any of the three environments.
source: We did not observe a significant correlation between absolute fitness and our pleiotriopic traits, using either parametric or non-parametric approaches, in any of our three environments (Table 7).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Table 7.

claim: While the GSL genes are causing pleiotropic effects, these pleiotropic effects are probably not driving the observed fitness consequences of the GSL genotypes in the field trials.
source: This indicates that while the GSL genes are causing pleiotropic effects, these pleiotropic effects are probably not driving the observed fitness consequences of the GSL genotypes in our field trials.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between fitness and pleiotropic traits.

claim: 18 distinct aliphatic GSL haplotypes were identified among the set of 144 natural Arabidopsis accessions.
source: This identified 18 distinct aliphatic GSL haplotypes among the set of 144 natural Arabidopsis accessions, observed at different frequencies (Figure 9 and Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the haplotype analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Comparing the population of observed vs expected GSL haplotype frequencies was highly non-random (p < 0.001).
source: Comparing the population of observed vs expected frequencies was highly non-random (p < 0.001) (Figure 9 and Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Specific multi-locus GSL genotypes occurred significantly more or less often than expected.
